learning_outcomes.statement: After Chapter 4 the learner can choose among int/float/Decimal/Fraction/complex for a given problem, explain why 0.1+0.2 != 0.3, and compare floats with math.isclose() instead of ==.
The learner can use math, random, secrets and statistics correctly, including knowing that random() must not be used for passwords or tokens.

reviewers.attestation: Read scripts/build_chapter_004.py in full (all lesson-builder functions), cross-checked every printed/claimed code result by executing the corresponding snippets under the project's own .venv (Python 3.14.6), verified two external claims (PEP 773 Windows installer timeline; pysh-shell.com/PyPI pysh-shell authenticity) via web search, and confirmed the canonical source sha256 matches the frozen M01 baseline exactly (no drift since baseline).

criteria.rationale: Every arithmetic, rounding, precision, Decimal/Fraction-from-float, and statistics claim in the chapter was independently executed and matched exactly; no factual error found across 22 lessons.
All numeric examples were reproduced under the project's declared Python 3.14.6, including version-sensitive floor-division and banker's-rounding behavior, with identical results.

The chapter precisely distinguishes int/float/complex as built-in literal types from Decimal/Fraction as stdlib classes requiring import, and correctly labels CPython small-int caching and refcounting-adjacent id() behavior as an implementation detail not to rely on.

The opener promises number bases, operators/precedence, division/modulo, powers, float precision, Decimal, Fraction, complex, math, random/secrets, statistics and three mini-projects; every promised topic is present with working, verified examples.

The chapter's normative claims (IEEE 754 binary64, PEP 8 reference, random vs secrets security boundary) are all traceable to well-established stdlib/standard behavior verified by direct execution rather than assumed.
04-05's summary_box lists observable outcomes (choose the right numeric type, explain 0.1+0.2, round/floor/ceil/trunc correctly) plus a decision_map the learner can reuse in future chapters.

Every new numeric tool (Decimal, Fraction, complex, random/secrets, statistics) is explicitly introduced with import and rationale before use; nothing relies on later-chapter concepts (conditionals, functions).

04-10 motivates //  and % with a concrete '17 candies among 5 children' scenario before the operators are formalized, and 04-13 motivates float imprecision with a 1/3-in-decimal analogy before IEEE 754 detail.
Deeper material (refcounting-style CPython caching caveat, IEEE 754 binary64 layout, pow() modular arithmetic) is explicitly marked optional/skippable and visually separated from the core path.

04-22's nine debugging labs and 04-05's three mini-projects (purchase calculator, time converter, geometry calculator) require transferring the whole chapter's tools to new, previously unseen problems, closing with a reusable decision_map.
The name/reference/immutability model from Chapter 3 is explicitly and correctly re-applied to numbers ('age = age + 1 rebinds, does not mutate') rather than re-defined inconsistently.
Cross-references to Chapter 3 (names, immutability) and forward references to later chapters (mutable list behavior, conditionals) are accurate and appropriately bounded as 'not yet covered'.

The 'float vs Decimal vs Fraction' comparison is deliberately repeated with increasing detail across 04-14/04-15/04-16 and consolidated once more in the final decision_map, each repetition adding new information rather than duplicating text.
All 22 section identifiers and their sidebar/practice-card IDs (04-01..04-22) are internally consistent with the notebook filenames in notebooks/chapter-04/, with no gap or collision.
